content: If a patient experiences hypersensitivity reactions while taking thiabendazole, the medication must be stopped immediately and should not be restarted. Thiabendazole therapy has been linked to erythema multiforme, and in severe cases, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fatalities have occurred. Since central nervous system (CNS) side effects are relatively common, patients should avoid activities that require mental alertness. Cases of jaundice, cholestasis, and parenchymal liver damage have been reported in patients treated with MINTEZOL (thiabendazole). In rare instances, liver damage has been severe enough to result in irreversible hepatic failure. Patients treated with MINTEZOL have also reported abnormal eye sensations, xanthopsia (yellow-tinted vision), blurred vision, dryness of mucous membranes, and Sicca syndrome. In some cases, these ocular side effects have persisted for over a year. Thiabendazole is generally not recommended as a first-line treatment for enterobiasis and should only be used in patients who have shown allergic reactions or resistance to other therapies. General Precautions: MINTEZOL is not appropriate for treating mixed infections involving Ascaris, as it may cause these worms to migrate. Supportive care is recommended for patients who are anemic, dehydrated, or malnourished before starting anthelmintic therapy. Patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction should be closely monitored during treatment. Thiabendazole should only be used in patients with a confirmed diagnosis of a susceptible worm infestation and should not be used prophylactically. Patient Information: Due to the frequent occurrence of CNS side effects, patients should avoid activities requiring mental alertness while taking this medication. Laboratory Monitoring: In rare cases, patients receiving MINTEZOL have experienced a temporary increase in liver function test results. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and Fertility: Animal studies involving thiabendazole at doses up to 15 times the usual human dose have not shown carcinogenic effects. Fertility was not adversely affected in mice at doses 2.5 times the human dose or in rats at doses equivalent to the human dose. Thiabendazole has shown no mutagenic activity in in vitro microbial mutagen tests, the micronucleus test, or in vivo host-mediated assays. Pregnancy (Category C): Reproductive and teratogenic studies in rabbits (at doses up to 15 times the human dose), rats (at doses equivalent to the human dose), and mice (at doses up to 2.5 times the human dose) have not demonstrated harm to the fetus. However, in a separate study in mice, cleft palate and axial skeletal defects were observed when thiabendazole was administered in olive oil at 10 times the human dose, though no defects were observed when the drug was given in an aqueous suspension at the same dose. There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Thiabendazole should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefits outweigh the potential risks to the fetus. Nursing Mothers: It is unknown whether thiabendazole is excreted in human breast milk. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the medication to the mother. Pediatric Use: The safety and efficacy of thiabendazole for treating Strongyloidiasis, Ascariasis, Uncinariasis, Trichuriasis, and Trichinosis in pediatric patients weighing less than 30 pounds have not been well established. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies of MINTEZOL have not included sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine whether their response differs from that of younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified significant differences between elderly and younger patients. In general, dosing for elderly patients should be cautious, starting at the lower end of the dosing range, due to the increased likelihood of reduced hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of other medical conditions or concurrent drug therapies. Since this drug is primarily metabolized by the liver and its metabolites are excreted by the kidneys, patients with impaired renal function may be at greater risk of toxicity. Therefore, renal function should be monitored, and dose adjustments may be necessary in elderly patients.
